title: The upper room (Mark 14:12–31)
hook: take, this is my body; this is my blood of the new testament

segments.voice: Yesterday, what she hath done: a woman broke a jar of perfume over Jesus's head, and he said she did what she could. Your line was she did what she could. Whose kindness did you tell? Today, supper. Day two hundred twenty-six.

It's the first day of the feast of Unleavened Bread, when the Passover lambs are sacrificed. The disciples ask where they should get the meal ready. Jesus sends two of them into the city with odd directions: you'll meet a man carrying a jar of water. Follow him. Wherever he goes in, ask the owner for the guest room. He'll show you a large upper room, furnished and ready. It all happens just as he said. That evening he arrives with the twelve. Catholics trace every Mass back to what happens at this table.
screen: `THE DAY OF THE PASSOVER LAMBS.` → `FOLLOW THE MAN WITH THE WATER JAR.` → `A LARGE UPPER ROOM, READY.`

segments.voice: First, the betrayal at the table. While they're reclining and eating, Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "one of you that eateth with me shall betray me." They're heartbroken, and one by one they ask him: "Is it I?" Nobody points at anyone else. Each one wonders about himself. Second, the bread. "And whilst they were eating, Jesus took bread; and blessing, broke, and gave to them, and said: Take ye. This is my body." Took, blessed, broke, gave. Mark used almost the same four actions at the two feedings in the wilderness, and some readers hear those baskets echo here. Third, the cup. He takes a cup, gives thanks, and they all drink from it. Then he says: "This is my blood of the new testament, which shall be shed for many." Testament here means covenant, a binding promise. At Sinai, Moses sealed God's covenant with blood. Now Jesus speaks of his own. Fourth, what Catholics believe. The Catholic Church teaches that at every Mass, when the priest speaks these words over bread and wine, they truly become the body and blood of Christ, while still looking like bread and wine. The Church calls this transubstantiation. Orthodox Christians also believe in a real change, and speak of it as a mystery; many Protestants understand the meal as a memorial or a spiritual presence. And notice the first word over the bread: take. In Mark, the bread is given to be received. Then they sing a hymn and walk out to the Mount of Olives, and Peter promises: "Although all shall be scandalized in thee, yet not I." Before the cock crows twice, Jesus tells him, you'll deny me three times.
screen: `ONE OF YOU WILL BETRAY ME. IS IT I?` · `TOOK, BLESSED, BROKE, GAVE.` · `THE BLOOD OF THE NEW COVENANT.` · `CATHOLICS TRACE EVERY MASS HERE.` · then, large: `TAKE YE. THIS IS MY BODY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember the last supper at your next meal. Right now, settle and breathe, and picture that room. Low tables, lamplight, thirteen people close together, the smell of bread. Now picture your next meal, wherever it will be. Decide that before you eat it, you'll pause for one breath and remember this table. If you pray, you can say grace, or simply say thank you. If you don't, just notice the bread in your hands and who made it. The bell holds the time.
The upper room. The borrowed guest room in Jerusalem where Jesus ate the last supper with the twelve, and said over bread: take, this is my body. Today's word.
Your line: take. Today, when something is offered, a meal, a hand, some help, don't refuse it. Take it, and say thank you. Day two hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: At every Catholic Mass the priest repeats Jesus's words over the bread and wine at the consecration, and Catholics receive Communion believing it is truly the body and blood of Christ; the Last Supper is remembered especially on Holy Thursday.

original.note: Greek: take (you all). the first word Jesus says over the bread in Mark.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus's last meal before he died.
what it means: bread and cup given as his body and blood, a new covenant, the table every Mass goes back to.
what a scholar hears: labete, touto estin to sōma mou; diathēkē, covenant, echoing the blood of the covenant at Sinai (Exodus 24:8).

notes: Douay-Rheims Mark 14:18, 14:19, 14:22, 14:24 and 14:29 given from memory; confirm wording.
Transubstantiation described per CCC 1376; the Orthodox and Protestant views summarized in one line each without ranking. Keeper should confirm fairness and accuracy.
The Missal's words of consecration are described, not quoted (the current English Missal translation is not public domain).
'The same four actions as the feedings': Mark 6:41 has took, blessed, broke, gave; 8:6 has took, gave thanks, broke, gave. Confirm the simplification.
The observation that a man carrying a water jar would be unusual is omitted as uncertain.

Editor review (2026-10-01): 'Every Mass in the world goes back to this table' now attributed to Catholics, not stated by the narrator; 'the same four actions' softened to 'almost the same' (8:6 has 'giving thanks'); 'the baskets were pointing here' softened to what readers hear; garbled 'Catholics say it simply: take' rewritten.
